historical_timeline.summary: Born in Beaufort County, South Carolina.
Moved to Philadelphia as a teenager; worked in a slaughterhouse.
Olympic heavyweight gold medal in Tokyo, with a broken left thumb; a cataract found in his left eye later that year.
Third fight of his rivalry, stopped before the fifteenth round when he could not see; vision 20/400 in the left eye.
Retired from boxing (one further bout in 1981).
Living in Philadelphia and running his gym; diabetes and high blood pressure reported publicly.
Diagnosed with liver cancer; hospice care at home in his last week.

claims.statement: Joe Frazier was born on January 12, 1944, in Beaufort County, South Carolina, the eleventh child of a sharecropping family.

source_links.locator: born in Beaufort, S.C., on Jan. 12, 1944

claims.statement: As a teenager he moved to Philadelphia, where he had relatives, and worked in a slaughterhouse, where he punched sides of beef in the cold room.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors his Philadelphia home and working life in the modern social history.

claims.statement: He won the heavyweight gold medal at the 1964 Olympic Games in Tokyo, fighting the final with a broken left thumb.

source_links.locator: fighting with an injured left thumb

claims.statement: Later in 1964 he learned that he had a cataract in his left eye; visually impaired, he turned professional anyway. The cataract grew worse, and by 1975, according to his eye doctor, his vision was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/400 in the left.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Reported during his life. Anchors the reduced vision in the left eye in the modern episode. Later accounts that he hid the eye from examiners appeared only after his death and are not used.

source_links.locator: learned he had cataracts in his left eye; visually impaired, he turned pro
20/50 in the right eye and 20/400 in the left

claims.statement: He became undisputed world heavyweight champion in February 1970 and held the title until January 1973, defending it four times; he retired in 1976 after a professional record of 32 wins, 4 losses and 1 draw, with 27 knockouts, and returned for a single bout in 1981.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors a long professional career with many blows to the head, the basis for brain-health care in the modern episode.

claims.statement: His three-fight rivalry in the 1970s included a 1971 victory that handed his opponent his first professional defeat; in the third fight, in Manila in 1975, he could no longer see, and his trainer would not let him come out for the fifteenth round.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; the opponent is not named in this record.

claims.statement: In later life he lived in Philadelphia, where he owned and ran a boxing gym, and he had financial trouble.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors his work at the gym and cost concerns in the modern social history.

source_links.locator: lives in Philadelphia, owns and runs a gym there
later had financial trouble and ended up running a gym

claims.statement: During his life it was reported publicly that he had diabetes and high blood pressure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern diabetes and hypertension; the duration, severity and treatment in the modern episode are synthetic.

source_links.locator: he has diabetes and high blood pressure

claims.statement: In October 2011 he was diagnosed with liver cancer; he was in and out of the hospital from early October and received hospice care at home in his last week.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode, as his manager and a family friend stated publicly. The modern episode contains no liver cancer; its teaching point is surveillance that can find liver cancer early.

claims.statement: He died on November 7, 2011, in Philadelphia, at 67, after a brief illness with liver cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, recorded in one plain sentence.

claims.statement: He published an autobiography, Smokin' Joe, in 1996.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His nickname, used here as an alias.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Type 2 diabetes and hypertension in a 64-year-old Black man, a former professional heavyweight boxer who runs a gym, managed under the ADA Standards of Care 2026, the 2025 AHA/ACC blood pressure guideline and the CMID monographs: A1c, kidney function by the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equation and urine albumin, lipids and a high-intensity statin, a GLP-1 receptor agonist with cardiovascular and kidney benefit, blood pressure to below 130/80 with home readings, eye and foot examinations, and cost and access. The yearly liver check finds a high FIB-4, and the AASLD 2023 MASLD guidance leads to elastography and a diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis from MASLD; under the AASLD 2023 hepatocellular carcinoma guidance he begins ultrasound with AFP every six months, the kind of surveillance that can find liver cancer early, with variceal screening, vaccines and no alcohol. Brain health in a former boxer is addressed with a documented cognitive screen and risk-factor care, and without a diagnosis of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which can be made only after death.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Frazier returns two weeks after intake with a week of home blood pressure readings, twice a day, averaging 146/90. He is taking metformin, lisinopril and the new atorvastatin without trouble. This morning he had liver elastography and a liver ultrasound, and he saw Dr. Deshpande of hepatology. He has had no swelling of the legs or abdomen, no black stools, no confusion and no yellowing. He drinks one or two beers on some weekends and agreed today to stop. He asked what a scarred liver means for his work at the gym.

ros.finding: No abdominal swelling, black stools or vomiting of blood
No muscle aches on atorvastatin
No confusion or day-night reversal

exam.finding: Well; blood pressure 148/90, pulse 74; weight 103.6 kg

assessment_plan.assessment: Liver stiffness 17.6 kPa with a controlled attenuation parameter of 318 dB/m; ultrasound shows a mildly nodular liver, a spleen of 13.4 cm and no focal lesion; AFP 4.2 ng/mL; INR 1.1; albumin 4.0 g/dL; bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL; platelets 138. Child-Pugh A (5 points), MELD 8. Hepatitis B surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody negative; hepatitis A antibody negative; hepatitis C antibody and HIV test nonreactive; iron studies and autoimmune tests normal. Dr. Deshpande agrees this is compensated cirrhosis from MASLD, with little alcohol
plan: Liver ultrasound with AFP every six months; the next in September
Upper endoscopy to screen for varices, because platelets below 150 and a stiffness of 17.6 kPa cannot rule out portal hypertension
No alcohol; no ibuprofen or naproxen; acetaminophen no more than 2 g a day
PCV20 and first doses of hepatitis A and B vaccines today

referral.pertinent_history: Former professional heavyweight boxer who runs a gym. Type 2 diabetes for about twelve years on metformin (A1c 8.4%); hypertension on lisinopril, above goal; LDL 132 mg/dL, HDL 38, triglycerides 210; BMI 31.4. Alcohol: one or two beers on some weekends (AUDIT-C 2); never smoked; no drug use. No history of jaundice, swelling or bleeding. Today: AST 48 and ALT 42 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 96, albumin 4.0 g/dL, bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, platelets 138, hemoglobin 14.2, creatinine 1.08 mg/dL (eGFR 77), urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 18 mg/g. questions: How advanced is the fibrosis, and is this MASLD?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Frazier, a 64-year-old former professional boxer, is seen at the request of Dr. Whitfield for a FIB-4 of 3.43 found at his yearly diabetes check. He feels well and has had no jaundice, abdominal or leg swelling, black stools, vomiting of blood or confusion. He drinks one or two beers on some weekends and has never drunk heavily. He has had diabetes for about twelve years and high blood pressure for many years. He has never had a blood transfusion or used injected drugs. He wants to keep working at his gym
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Whitfield's intake note and results: AST 48, ALT 42 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 96, albumin 4.0 g/dL, bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, platelets 138, creatinine 1.08 mg/dL, FIB-4 3.43. Today: transient elastography with a median liver stiffness of 17.6 kPa (interquartile range 14%) and a controlled attenuation parameter of 318 dB/m; ultrasound with a coarse, echogenic, mildly nodular liver, a spleen of 13.4 cm, a patent portal vein, no ascites and no focal lesion; INR 1.1; AFP 4.2 ng/mL. Hepatitis B surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody negative; hepatitis A antibody negative; hepatitis C antibody and HIV nonreactive; ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies negative

exam.finding: Well; blood pressure 148/90, pulse 74; BMI 31.3
Liver edge firm at the costal margin; spleen tip not felt; no ascites
No jaundice, spider angiomas or palmar erythema
No asterixis

assessment.assessment: Steatosis with diabetes, obesity, low HDL and high triglycerides and little alcohol meets the definition of MASLD. Other causes have been excluded by the tests above

A FIB-4 above 2.67 followed by a liver stiffness of 17.6 kPa, with platelets of 138, a nodular liver and a large spleen, is consistent with compensated advanced chronic liver disease, most likely cirrhosis. A biopsy would not change management. Child-Pugh A (5 points), MELD 8. There is no sign of decompensation

Cirrhosis from MASLD carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma high enough to justify surveillance by ultrasound with AFP every six months; today's baseline is clear and of good quality. Surveillance on time is what finds cancer when it can still be cured

A stiffness between 15 and 25 kPa with platelets below 150 cannot rule clinically significant portal hypertension in or out, so an upper endoscopy to look for varices is advised; a beta-blocker would be started if varices needing treatment are found

A GLP-1 receptor agonist such as semaglutide is favored: it lowers glucose and weight, has cardiovascular and kidney benefit, and improves steatohepatitis. Metformin is safe to continue in compensated cirrhosis with normal kidney function, and atorvastatin is safe and beneficial. Sulfonylureas and insulin are not needed and carry a risk of low blood sugar

recommendations: Liver ultrasound with AFP every six months, starting with today's baseline
Upper endoscopy to screen for varices within the next six weeks; if none are found and the liver injury continues, repeat in two years
Start semaglutide and increase it as tolerated; continue metformin and atorvastatin 40 mg
Aim for 7 to 10% weight loss over a year
No alcohol at all; no ibuprofen or naproxen; acetaminophen no more than 2 g a day
Hepatitis A and B vaccine series and PCV20 now; influenza, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines in season
Albumin, bilirubin, platelets and kidney function every six months; repeat elastography in one year
Teach the warning signs of decompensation: abdominal or leg swelling, black stools or vomiting of blood, confusion, yellowing
